name: Rust
summary: A systems language and toolchain whose compiler lowers source through several typed intermediate representations, performs ownership-aware analyses, and uses a query system to support incremental compilation.

features.name: Ownership and borrowing
features.description: Rust's ownership model assigns each value an owner and uses borrowing rules to govern references, enabling memory-safety guarantees without a garbage collector when the program satisfies the language rules.
benefits: Moves important memory-safety checks into compilation
Avoids requiring a tracing garbage collector for the ownership model
costs: Programs must satisfy ownership and lifetime constraints at compile time
The model can require redesign of APIs that would be straightforward with shared mutable state

features.name: Multi-stage compiler intermediate representations
features.description: The Rust compiler uses a sequence of representations including tokens, AST, HIR, THIR, MIR, and LLVM IR. MIR is a control-flow-oriented representation used for borrow checking, dataflow checks, optimization, and constant evaluation.
benefits: Matches each analysis to a representation with suitable abstraction and detail
Provides explicit boundaries for lowering, checking, optimization, and code generation
costs: Maintaining multiple representations and lowering steps increases compiler complexity
Information and source correspondence must be preserved across transformations

features.name: Query-driven incremental compilation
features.description: Rust organizes many compiler steps as queries that call one another and cache results, including on disk, so recompilation can reuse work whose inputs have not changed.
benefits: Reduces redundant work after localized source changes
Makes dependencies between compiler computations explicit enough to cache
costs: Cache invalidation and query dependency tracking add implementation complexity
Not every compiler step is query-driven or cacheable, so the abstraction is not complete

mathematical_views.question: How does a Rust program move from source syntax to representations suitable for type checking, borrow checking, and code generation?
assumptions: Each representation is modeled as a typed relation to the preceding representation
Lowering preserves the relevant language semantics while making implicit operations explicit
The view abstracts diagnostics, macro implementation details, and target-specific code generation

mathematical_views.question: Which compiler computations can be reused when source inputs change?
assumptions: Queries are vertices and calls or input dependencies are directed edges
A cached result is reusable only when the query system considers its relevant inputs unchanged
The model does not claim that every compiler operation is cached or that cache reuse preserves a particular wall-clock cost

benefits: Compile-time memory-safety boundary without a tracing collector
costs: Ownership and lifetime constraints increase API and program-design burden

benefits: Specialized analyses over representations with appropriate abstraction
costs: Multiple lowering boundaries increase maintenance and source-mapping cost
Dependency tracking, cache storage, and invalidation complicate the compiler
